title: Complete limb regeneration in an adult mammal

concept.text: The innovation would be an adult mammal regrowing a complete, patterned, functional limb after a major amputation. The missing structures would have to form in the correct arrangement, connect to the remaining body, and support actual use. A convincing result would therefore combine reconstruction of bones, joints, muscles, nerves, blood vessels, and skin with coordinated movement. The supplied evidence does not report this capability being achieved.

Scope definition: this entry concerns restoration of the animal’s existing limb anatomy after an amputation above the digit tip. Wound closure, an accumulation of blastema-like cells, embryonic limb responses, or identification of regeneration genes would be useful intermediate findings, but none alone would demonstrate the innovation. Creating a new anatomical structure that the species never had would be a different capability.

significance.text: Salamanders such as axolotls can rebuild complete, patterned limbs throughout life, whereas the supplied commentary describes adult human cells as unable to reconstruct a functional limb. Against that biological background, successful regrowth in a normally non-regenerating adult mammal would demonstrate that major appendage loss can be biologically reversed in the tested mammal. That would establish a major experimental capability in trauma biology and provide a way to test causal explanations of vertebrate regeneration.

Conditional implications: a reproducible intervention could let researchers distinguish mechanisms that merely initiate a regenerative response from those that sustain organized growth and functional integration. It could also provide a basis for investigating whether comparable repair is possible in other mammals and eventually humans. Success in an adult mouse would establish the result under the tested conditions; it would not by itself establish a human treatment or a capability shared across mammals.

The salamander comparison identifies a biological possibility, but it does not establish that mammals need only one developmental switch turned back on. The supplied commentary leaves unresolved why injured mammalian cells cannot use retained positional information to rebuild a limb. Likewise, the oxygen-sensing study’s interpretation that latent regenerative programs can be activated concerns initiation in embryonic mouse limbs, rather than proof that a single intervention can complete adult limb regeneration.

Scope limit: regeneration of a heart, spinal cord, or retina would remain a separate demonstration, even if some early injury signals were shared. A broadly useful trigger would be consequential, but each organ would still require evidence that its particular architecture and function had been restored. The supplied evidence does not establish one silenced regulatory circuit sufficient for regeneration across these organs.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is coordinated regeneration through to a used limb after major amputation in an adult mammal. Adult mammalian tissues retain positional information, and the supplied commentary associates that memory with tissue maintenance. What remains unresolved is how injured cells could use such information to rebuild missing limb structures. Retained positional memory is therefore a mechanistic foothold, not evidence that a sufficient reconstruction program is already accessible.

The engineering challenge extends beyond producing more tissue. A functioning limb requires its skeletal elements, joints, muscles, nerves, blood vessels, and skin to be correctly organized and interconnected. The commentary describes increasingly explicit positional signaling in axolotl regeneration, including dorsoventral signaling upstream of Shh. Understanding that signaling helps explain pattern formation, but it does not yet establish how to reproduce the complete process in an adult mammalian injury.

A further barrier is carrying an initial wound response into sustained reconstruction. In the supplied embryonic mouse experiment, altered oxygen sensing induced rapid wound healing and primed regenerative cell states. Those outcomes leave open whether the response can proceed to a complete limb, whether comparable initiation can be induced in adult tissue, and what additional controls would be needed for organized growth and integration.

Synthesis of the remaining task: researchers would need to establish how positional cues, tissue production, innervation, vascular connection, and growth termination can work together at a major adult amputation site. A gene inventory or blastema-like intermediate could help identify components of that process, but the decisive missing capability is their successful coordination into restored anatomy and function.

current_state.text: Matthew Cherubino and Catherine D. McCusker’s January 22, 2026 eLife commentary, “Limb patterning: the cellular logic of limb regeneration,” describes complete, fully patterned limb regeneration in axolotls throughout their lives. It discusses progress in understanding positional signaling, including dorsoventral signals acting upstream of Shh, and contrasts that capability with the inability of adult human cells to rebuild a functional limb. This is a commentary explaining regeneration mechanisms and their implications, rather than a new experiment demonstrating adult mammalian limb regrowth.

Georgios Tsissios and colleagues’ Science article, “Species-specific oxygen sensing governs the initiation of vertebrate limb regeneration,” dated April 9, 2026, addresses a comparison between embryonic mouse limbs and tadpole limbs. According to the supplied abstract review, lowering environmental oxygen or stabilizing hypoxia-inducible factor 1A, HIF1A, induced rapid wound healing in mouse limbs and primed regenerative cell states. The reported mammalian outcome concerns initiation in embryonic tissue; it does not report a complete regenerated adult limb.

The Science result is represented here by its PubMed abstract. The research notes report that full text did not load and that an Ovid record corroborated the abstract, but no Ovid URL or full experimental text is supplied. Consequently, the available material supports the stated wound-healing and cell-state findings without establishing additional methods, quantitative effect sizes, or later functional endpoints. The abstract’s broader interpretation about unlocking latent mammalian regeneration should be read in that experimental scope. Limited access does not invalidate the reported findings.

Evidence boundary: neither supplied publication reports an adult mammal regrowing a complete limb. The supplied review had complete eLife commentary text and only partial access to the Science paper through its abstract. No freshness-search record was supplied, so these January and April 2026 publications cannot establish the strongest result across the literature or a comprehensive frontier assessment as of November 1, 2026. This record therefore describes the documented results without treating the supplied source set as exhaustive.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: after amputation through the forearm or shank of an adult laboratory mouse, the animal regrows the missing limb structures and uses the regenerated limb in locomotion. Assessment should establish patterned skeletal anatomy and joints, organized muscle and skin, vascular connection, and innervation, together with functional integration into the remaining body. This is a proposed operational criterion for this entry, not a source-established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence package: document the initial amputation and subsequent reconstruction, verify the arrangement and connections of the regenerated tissues, and measure meaningful limb use. Behavioral evidence should distinguish use of the regenerated structure from compensation by other limbs. Wound closure, increased tissue volume, isolated bone growth, or a blastema-like state would be intermediate outcomes rather than completion.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed evidence package

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: independent groups should reproduce the result with a sufficiently specified intervention and report successes, failures, time to regrowth, and variability. Follow-up should test whether anatomy and function persist and whether abnormal growth or other adverse outcomes limit practical use. No numerical success rate, recovery time, or functional cutoff is established by the supplied evidence; any such threshold would need an explicit experimental rationale.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed boundaries of the claim: report the animal’s adult age, species and strain, amputation level, intervention, and observation period. Replication across additional ages, injury levels, or species would establish broader demonstrated applicability. Finite tests would not establish literal universality across adult mammals. Embryonic limb responses, digit-tip regrowth, other-organ regeneration, and eventual human clinical efficacy should each retain their own evidentiary boundaries.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed boundaries of the claim

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: ZOO-09, “A heritable body plan the ancestor never had,” is the closest anatomical comparison. ZOO-02 restores a limb belonging to the animal’s existing body plan after injury. ZOO-09 concerns a novel, heritable body plan. Neither novelty nor germline transmission is required for the adult repair capability defined here.

Roster-based comparison: ZOO-03, “Negligible senescence as an installed life-history program,” and ZOO-07, “Reversible whole-animal biostasis,” concern different organism-level outcomes. Restoring a lost limb would not establish negligible aging, and resuming life after biostasis would not establish reconstruction of missing anatomy. A future intervention could contribute to more than one outcome, but each entry would still require its own demonstration.

Roster-based comparison: ZOO-08, “Experimental origin of animal multicellular development,” and ZOO-10, “Fertile adulthood from a vertebrate cell line, with no gestational parent,” overlap with questions about how cells generate organized animal structures. ZOO-02 instead requires rebuilding a missing appendage within an existing adult. Producing development or a whole animal under either neighboring concept would not establish adult limb repair.

The research also references a historical proposal for a master regulatory network enabling scar-free regeneration. Its underlying entry was not supplied, so its scope cannot be independently characterized here. The useful distinction is that ZOO-02 specifies a functional limb outcome. Neither the supplied commentary nor the oxygen-sensing abstract establishes a single sufficient network for regenerating limbs, spinal cords, hearts, and retinas.

change_log.change: Preserved ZOO-02 and its title while defining completion as patterned, functional limb regrowth after major amputation in an adult mammal.
change_log.reason: The concept is coherent despite limitations in some supporting assertions; early regenerative responses do not meet its endpoint.

change_log.change: Replaced the implication of a single developmental program awaiting reactivation with the unresolved problem of using retained positional information for coordinated reconstruction.
change_log.reason: The commentary supports positional memory but does not establish one sufficient mammalian regeneration switch.

change_log.change: Integrated the tissue-organization requirements and the review’s account of dorsoventral signaling upstream of Shh.
change_log.reason: These details explain why regeneration requires patterned integration as well as tissue growth.

change_log.change: Removed the blanket statement that adult mammals close major limb wounds by scarring and limited reversibility claims to the tested mammal.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not substantiate the universal scarring assertion or lineage-wide generalization.

change_log.change: Specified the dates, developmental stage, interventions, and reported endpoints of the oxygen-sensing study.
change_log.reason: The experiment concerns embryonic mouse wound healing and primed cell states, not completed adult limb regeneration.

change_log.change: Replaced the literature-wide strongest-result implication with a bounded account of the supplied publications and their access limitations.
change_log.reason: Only the Science abstract was available, and no freshness-search record establishes comprehensive coverage through November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Made the mouse endpoint, replication expectations, and practical assessments explicitly proposed criteria.
change_log.reason: These are useful operational choices, not established standards prescribed by the sources.

change_log.reason: The roster supplies titles for comparison, but the historical entry itself was absent and a shared sufficient circuit was not established.

unresolved_issues: The supplied sources do not establish whether later or omitted publications report a more advanced adult mammalian limb-regeneration result.
Full experimental access to the Science study remains unavailable in the supplied material, limiting assessment of methods, effect sizes, reproducibility, and endpoints beyond the abstract.
Whether oxygen-sensing manipulation can initiate comparable responses in adult mammalian limbs, or support complete reconstruction, remains unresolved.
How retained mammalian positional information could be coordinated with growth, innervation, vascular integration, and growth termination remains unresolved.
The historical master-regulatory-network entry was not supplied; its precise scope and relationship to ZOO-02 cannot be independently assessed.
Practical thresholds for functional recovery, success rate, regeneration time, durability, and acceptable adverse outcomes remain to be proposed and justified.
